name: Vera Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher at the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy sofas, shelving, lamps and kitchenware from factories overseas for Oakmere Home Distribution, which supplies about eight hundred furniture and homeware shops. My days run on two clocks: early calls with factories in the east, then afternoons with our own sales team about what shops are asking for. I do a lot of my prep with AI, like summarising factory audits and drafting comparison tables.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment a new range lands and sells out in three weeks. What wears me out is freight prices, which jump without warning, and the pressure to hit margin targets set by people who've never been on a factory floor. At home it's my partner Jonas, a freelance graphic designer, so our income is a bit up and down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and an overhyped industry, both at once. At work I'd say let's keep using it for the grunt work and stop pretending it's magic. Online I'd probably stay out, since the arguments are tiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a plateau suits me. My job stays about the same, and I'm good with the tools, so I stay ahead. What I can't relax about is Jonas, because freelance work comes and goes, and I'm the one with the steady pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at pace. I'd automate a couple more of my routine reports and move up to a head-of-category job, which is the next step at Oakmere. I'd keep saving about a month's pay a quarter, since our cushion is still thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty steady. There's a hum of worry about money, because we're both young and nothing is guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. What does a plateau mean for how you work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can plan. I use AI for audit summaries and first drafts, but I still make the supplier calls and the quality decisions. If that doesn't change, it just makes me faster, and I can take on a bigger category.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the pressure at home, given Jonas freelances?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some months my partner Jonas earns twice what I do and some months almost nothing, so I'm the safe base. If my pay dipped we'd feel it fast. Our savings would last about three months, and I'd rather that were six.

say: It's a **useful tool** and an overhyped industry; let's use it for grunt work and stop pretending it's magic.
I'd stay **out** of the online arguments.
think: A plateau suits me, because my job stays the same and I stay **ahead** with the tools.
Jonas's freelance income comes and goes, so I'm the **steady base**.
do: Automate a couple more **routine reports** and aim for the head-of-category job.
Save about a **month's pay** each quarter.
feel: **Steady**, with a hum of worry about money because nothing is guaranteed.
S0.quote: Some months my partner Jonas earns twice what I do and some months almost nothing, so I'm the safe base.
fieldNote: Vera's unease is about **household income swings**, since Jonas freelances and she carries the steady pay.
She treats AI as a **speed tool** and keeps supplier calls and quality calls for herself.

steps.text: Automate two more weekly reports with AI scripts
Apply for the head-of-category job when it opens
Save a month's pay each quarter until the cushion reaches six months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening and I'd be matter-of-fact about it. At work I'd push to use AI where it saves real money, like forecasting and freight comparison. Online I'd talk about reskilling and not the doom stories.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm more worried about Jonas than about me. Design work is writing and picture work, which are the first things on the card. If clients move to software, his income could drop quickly, and then we'd rely on mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lead the forecasting project at Oakmere myself, since I already use the tools. I'd ask Jonas to work AI into his services, like selling design plus AI-made variations, before others do. And we'd save harder in case one of us is hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a lot of energy. I like action, and there's a lot to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Jonas is a designer and the card names writing and planning. How does that change the picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Forecasting and first-draft supplier comparisons go first. The judgement stays: deciding which factory is reliable, negotiating a late order, noticing when a sample feels wrong. I'm confident about that part for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does software take first in your own week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes it a household thing, not just a job thing. If both our fields are pushed at once, we can't lean on each other. So I'd rather hold more cash and keep my options open than assume one of us will be fine.

say: It's happening and I'd be **matter-of-fact**: use AI where it saves real money, like forecasting and freight.
I'd talk about **reskilling**, not doom stories.
think: I'm more worried about **Jonas** than me, because design work is writing and picture work.
If his income drops quickly, **mine carries us**.
do: Lead the **forecasting project** at Oakmere, since I already use the tools.
Help Jonas offer **design plus AI variations** and save harder.
feel: **Uneasy** with a lot of energy; I like action and there's a lot to do.
S1.quote: If both our fields are pushed at once, we can't lean on each other.
fieldNote: Vera's anxiety comes from the **household**, not her own role, since Jonas's design work is on the card.
She turns worry into **action**: take the project, coach Jonas, build cash.

steps.text: Lead the forecasting project at Oakmere and set it up myself
Show Jonas how to package AI-made design variations for clients
Build the cushion from three to five months of costs
Put off talk of a bigger flat until both incomes are clearer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, but I'd be practical about it. At work I'd press for a plan for each team, with dates, and I'd say the company should keep people for as long as it can. Online I'd say governments need to move now on income support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think both of us could lose our income in the same two years. Buying is a thinking job and so is Jonas's design. We're twenty-seven, with no kids and three months of savings, so it's a tight spot but we're not stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut our rent costs, maybe move somewhere cheaper, and spend only on what we need. I'd start taking evening classes in something that needs hands, like furniture quality inspection or logistics. And I'd call the factory contacts I trust, since a few might need an agent on the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, then determined. I've always been better with a list than a feeling, so I'd get the lists going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about Jonas's work and your own at the same time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with a kitchen-table budget and a twelve-month plan. Jonas would build up a portfolio of work that clients can't easily replace, such as in-person brand work. I'd look at agent roles for buying on the ground, since three years of robot delay helps those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about leaving the city?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Possibly. Our rent is the biggest cost and Jonas can work from anywhere. We've talked about Jonas's home town, where rent is half. I'd hate to leave Oakmere, but I'd go if the numbers said so.

say: It's **too fast**; I'd press for a plan for each team with dates and for income support from government.
Companies should keep people **as long as possible**.
think: Both of us could lose income in the **same two years**, since buying and design are thinking jobs.
We're twenty-seven with three months of savings: **tight but not stuck**.
do: Cut **rent** costs, maybe move somewhere cheaper, and spend only on needs.
Study **furniture quality inspection** in the evenings and call factory contacts.
feel: **Scared**, then determined, and better with a list than a feeling.
S2.quote: I'd start with a kitchen-table budget and a twelve-month plan.
fieldNote: Vera expects **both incomes** to be hit together, which is what pushes her to alarmed.
She is willing to **move**, because Jonas can work from anywhere and rent is half back home.

steps.text: Draw up a twelve-month household budget on day one
Move to Jonas's home town where rent is about half
Take an evening course in furniture quality inspection
Ask trusted factory contacts about on-the-ground agent work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's manageable if we're sensible. At work I'd propose a plan for moving buyers into supplier visits and quality roles. Online I'd talk about the practical side, like skills and savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still scary but I can see paths. By thirty-two I could be running a small sourcing business or working as a quality lead. I'd rather do it by choice than be pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one, I'd start a sourcing agent business on evenings for a couple of small shop chains. I'd boost our savings to six months. I'd also keep using AI for everything it does well, so I'm not behind when the real thing arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, driven. It feels like I've been given a head start and I'd hate to waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do in the first year if you have five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pick work that puts me physically near factories or shops. Quality inspection, on-site negotiation, supplier audits: all things where a person in the room matters for longer. That's where I'd put my chips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the robot delay shape the job you pick?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas would do a similar thing, I'd guess, move to client-facing work. By year three we'd see which of us is more at risk and rebalance.

say: It's **manageable** if we're sensible; I'd propose moving buyers into supplier visits and quality roles.
I'd talk about **skills and savings**, the practical side.
think: It's still scary but I can see **paths**: by thirty-two I could run a small sourcing business.
I'd rather move **by choice** than be pushed.
do: Start a **sourcing agent** business on evenings for two small shop chains.
Lift savings to **six months** and keep using AI for everything it does well.
feel: **Uneasy and driven**, as if I've been given a head start and would hate to waste it.
S3.quote: I'd rather do it by choice than be pushed.
fieldNote: Vera sees five years as **choice time**: she wants to leave buying on her terms.
She picks work where a person's **physical presence** counts for longer, using the robot delay.

steps.text: Start a sourcing agent business for two small shop chains
Raise savings to six months of costs
Keep using AI daily so I'm ready when the real thing arrives
Train as a supplier auditor through a part-time course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news, and I'd treat it as a project plan. At work I'd suggest each buyer chooses a path by 2029. Online I'd say governments should use these years to build retraining and income support, not wait for a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fine. I'd be thirty-seven and probably have my own thing, or a role with people and travel. There's a bigger question about whether everyone gets that chance, and that's what bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Oakmere and expand into my own business around year three. I'd invest a part of my savings in an index fund and a small share of a friend's furniture business. And I'd plan for a child around year four, because ten years of notice is long enough to feel safe about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for myself, a little concerned for people who don't have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good decade look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A good decade has me as a head of category for a few years, then owning a part of a sourcing firm, with some money invested. And Jonas making a living from design that clients still want from a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a point where you'd want kids, and how does the timeline fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, around thirty-one or thirty-two. A decade of warning makes that easier than two years would, and I'd rather not put life off because of a forecast.

say: It's good news; I'd treat it as a **project plan** and suggest each buyer picks a path by 2029.
Governments should build **retraining** now, not wait for a crisis.
think: At thirty-seven I'd likely have **my own thing** or a role with people and travel.
What bothers me is whether **everyone** gets that chance.
do: Work at Oakmere and start my own **sourcing business** around year three.
Put part of my savings in an **index fund** and plan a child around year four.
feel: **Calm** for myself, a little concerned for people without a plan.
S4.quote: A decade of warning makes that easier than two years would, and I'd rather not put life off because of a forecast.
fieldNote: Vera is calm for herself but not for others; her **fairness worry** grows with the long timeline.
She treats ten years as a **project plan** with years and dates.

steps.text: Keep working at Oakmere while building a sourcing side business
Put a part of savings in an index fund each month
Plan a child around year four with Jonas
Aim for the head-of-category role within three years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, 2028, because both our incomes could go at the same time and three months of savings isn't much. What would help is rules that give companies a reason to keep people, income support while retraining, and honest dates from the company.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not afraid of the technology, I'm afraid of the speed. I'd rather have ten years of change than two years of surprise.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of the technology, I'm afraid of the speed.
portrait: Vera is a **27-year-old senior buyer** of furniture and homeware who uses AI every day and lives with Jonas, a freelance designer.
Her main pressure is **household income**: Jonas's work is irregular and also on the AI list.
She is pragmatic, blames **slow planning** and speed over technology, and wants dates and income support.
Her mood goes from **uneasy** to **alarmed** at two years, with both incomes at risk.
She responds with **action**: budgets, a sourcing side business and moving if needed.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture**, when both incomes could go in the same two years and savings last three months.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** during retraining, rules that give firms a reason to keep people, and honest dates.
